A.justification: Most exhaustive enumeration of all required pieces (branded IDs, per-step unions, events, phase-based reducer, never-check) and avoids `as`/`any` in the transition logic. However, it maintains two parallel, unconnected type models (StepDataMap vs WizardState), uses confusing phase naming (e.g. 'shippingComplete' = on billing step), and the two invalid transitions are asserted as unrepresentable rather than rigorously proven at the type level.

B.justification: Clean, readable before/after with correct unique-symbol branding and a coherent step-discriminated union. But the generic `WizardAction<Next>` is collapsed when used, and — critically — 'submitting while dirty' is enforced by a runtime `if (state.dirty) return null` guard plus `as ContactInfo` casts, not by compile-time unrepresentability, so it misses the hardest requirement.

C.justification: Covers all sections but the design is runtime-guard driven (`if (state.step.kind !== ...) throw`), uses many `as` casts (e.g. `merged as PersonalInfoData`), declares unused unique symbols while actually branding with string literals, and defines but never wires `Result`/`StepIndex`. The invalid transitions are blocked at runtime, not made unrepresentable at compile time.

D.justification: Has a genuinely interesting idea — encoding transitions via `from`/`to` literal-number fields — and clean branded IDs. But the exhaustiveness check is technically broken: it switches on the string `` `${state.step}-${action.kind}` `` yet asserts `const _exhaustiveCheck: never = action`, where `action` is still the full `WizardAction` union, so this would not compile. The `from`/`to` fields are also not tied to the source state, so invalid transitions aren't actually prevented at the type level.

E.justification: Uses `as WizardState`/`as StepAddress`/`as OrderId` casts on nearly every return plus placeholder values (`"" as StepId`), which defeats the whole point of the exercise. The `completedSteps` tuple idea is promising but is undermined by slice/casts, and the design still permits `GO_BACK` from confirmation→payment→shipping, contradicting the 'no going back after payment' requirement. The compile-time proof is effectively absent.

raw_result.pairwise_analysis: A and B are the strongest, both delivering complete before/after models with correct branded IDs and discriminated unions; A edges out B because it avoids `as` casts in the transition logic and frames transitions as compile-time unrepresentability, whereas B falls back to a runtime `if (state.dirty) return null` guard that does not satisfy the 'prove at compile time' requirement. D distinguishes itself with an explicit `from`/`to` transition graph but ships a broken never-check (asserting `never` on a variable that is still the full union), while C relies on runtime guards and pervasive casts plus unused helper types. E ranks last because its heavy `as WizardState` casts and placeholder values erase type safety, and its state machine still allows back-navigation after payment, directly contradicting one of the two invalid transitions that were supposed to be made unrepresentable.
